title: You Put an Extra $30,000 a Year Into a Mega Backdoor Roth. It Could Grow to Roughly $1.23 Million in 20 Years.
summary: A mega backdoor Roth can help you save far more in tax-free retirement accounts, if your 401(k) plan allows it. Here's an example.
body_markdown:
A[mega backdoor Roth](https://smartasset.com/retirement/mega-backdoor-roth) lets some workers boost their retirement savings by making additional after-tax contributions to their 401(k) and then moving that money into a Roth account. Depending on your plan’s rules and how much your employer contributes, this strategy could more than double what you save each year. Here’s how an extra $30,000 annually may grow to $1.23 million in two decades.


## How a Mega Backdoor Roth Might Help Save Extra Money


Some companies let employees put money they’ve already paid taxes on into their 401(k). Doing so may help you save more for retirement than the regular 401(k) contribution limit allows. It can also allow you to use a mega backdoor Roth, which is a strategy that puts more of your money into a Roth account so it could grow and potentially get withdrawn tax-free in retirement.


For 2026, the basic 401(k) employee[contribution limit is $24,500](https://smartasset.com/retirement/maximum-401k-contributions) , while the overall limit on contributions from all sources is $72,000, not counting[catch-up contributions](https://smartasset.com/retirement/all-about-catch-up-contributions) .1 For 2027, those limits go up to $25,500 and $75,000, respectively.2 After accounting for your regular contribution and any employer contributions, the amount left under the overall limit can be used for[after-tax contributions](https://smartasset.com/retirement/after-tax-401k-contributions) . The table shows one way the 2027 numbers could work:


Contribution Source Amount **Available After-Tax Contribution Space**


Employee contribution $25,500 $49,500


Employer contributions $19,500 $30,000


After-tax contribution $30,000 $0


Not every plan allows voluntary after-tax contributions, and a[mega backdoor Roth strategy](https://smartasset.com/retirement/mega-backdoor-roth-limit) only works if your plan also offers a way to convert or[roll those contributions into a Roth account](https://smartasset.com/retirement/rollover-401k-to-roth-ira) . Any investment earnings on after-tax dollars are generally taxable when moved into a Roth, so converting quickly can help limit the tax bill. Your plan’s summary description and the benefits administrator could confirm whether these features are available.


**A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=google_discover_referral&utm_campaign=dp_rollovers_conversions&utm_content=putanextra30000ayearintomegabackdoorrothcouldgrowto123millionin20years_a) can help you calculate how much room you have for after-tax contributions each year and combine that strategy with your overall retirement plan.**


## Turning $30,000 Annually Into Roughly $1.23 Million


To see how a mega backdoor Roth could add up, let’s assume that you put $30,000 into a Roth account at the end of each year over two decades. This would add up to $600,000 in total contributions ($30,000 × 20). The table compares how much your nest egg could grow at an average 7% return annually:


Year Total Contributions Calculation Estimated Account Balance Investment Growth


5 $150,000 $30,000 × \[(1.07⁵ − 1) ÷ 0.07\] $172,522 $22,522


10 $300,000 $30,000 × \[(1.07¹⁰ − 1) ÷ 0.07\] $414,493 $114,493


15 $450,000 $30,000 × \[(1.07¹⁵ − 1) ÷ 0.07\] $753,871 $303,871


20 $600,000 $30,000 × \[(1.07²⁰ − 1) ÷ 0.07\] $1,229,865 $629,865


After five years, $150,000 in contributions would have grown by 15% ($22,522). In a decade, that gain climbs to about 38% of your contributions ($114,493), followed by $303,871 in 15 years and $629,865 at the end of two decades.


This example excludes fees, taxes on any earnings before conversion and changes in investment returns over time. If the[Roth distribution qualifies for tax-free treatment](https://smartasset.com/retirement/roth-ira-qualified-distribution) , you could withdraw the $1,229,865 without[federal income tax](https://smartasset.com/taxes/income-taxes) . This is generally allowed after reaching age 59 ½ and satisfying the applicable five-year rule.


If you had invested the same retirement savings in a[taxable brokerage account](https://smartasset.com/investing/when-you-should-use-a-taxable-brokerage-account) instead, dividends could create taxes along the way and investment gains could be subject to[capital gains tax](https://smartasset.com/investing/capital-gains-tax-calculator) after a sell.


## When a Mega Backdoor Roth Makes Sense for a Nest Egg


A mega backdoor Roth might be an effective savings strategy when you already[max out your regular 401(k) contribution limit](https://smartasset.com/retirement/how-to-max-out-401k) and earn too much to contribute directly to a Roth IRA. In 2027, Roth IRA eligibility phases out between $158,000 and $173,000 of income for single filers and between $250,000 and $260,000 for married couples filing jointly.


In that case, a mega backdoor Roth could let you add up to $49,500 more in 2027 ($75,000 − $25,500), though any employer contributions would lower that amount, and your plan has to allow it. Time will also matter, since fewer years of compounding leave less room for your savings to grow.


**A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=google_discover_referral&utm_campaign=dp_rollovers_conversions&utm_content=putanextra30000ayearintomegabackdoorrothcouldgrowto123millionin20years_a) can help you decide whether a mega backdoor Roth fits your retirement savings goals and compare other strategies.**
